lesson.title: Familiarity Breeds Liking: The Mere Exposure Effect
lesson.summary: The mere exposure effect is the finding that simply being exposed to something repeatedly, a face, a song, a word, tends to increase our liking for it, even when we're not consciously aware we've encountered it before.
lesson.body:
Robert Zajonc ran a series of influential studies published in 1968 showing something that seems almost too simple to be true: mere repeated exposure to a stimulus, with no reward, no new information, and nothing but the exposure itself, tends to make people like that stimulus more. In his experiments, participants were shown things like Chinese-like characters, made up words, or photographs of faces varying numbers of times, and stimuli that had been shown more often were consistently rated more favorably afterward than stimuli shown fewer times or not at all, even when participants could not reliably recall having seen the more familiar ones before.

Why would simple repetition breed liking? The leading explanation involves what psychologists call processing fluency. Each time we encounter a stimulus, it becomes slightly easier and faster for our mind to process the next time, and that increased ease of processing itself tends to feel subtly pleasant, a feeling that we then tend to misattribute to the stimulus itself rather than to the fact that we have simply seen it before. This connects directly to top-down processing, since prior exposure is one of the most basic ways that past experience shapes present perception. We are not perceiving the song or the face fresh each time. Our perception of it is colored by everything we have already processed about it, including how many times we have processed it before.

The mere exposure effect shows up constantly outside the laboratory. It is a large part of why advertisers repeat jingles, logos, and slogans long after most viewers could recite them from memory, since familiarity itself nudges preference upward. It helps explain why political candidates with greater name recognition tend to poll better even among voters who know little about their actual positions, and why a coworker or a piece of music you found unremarkable or even mildly irritating at first can grow on you simply through repeated contact. The effect is not unlimited, though. Extremely frequent exposure to the same stimulus can plateau or even reverse into boredom or irritation, and mere exposure tends to work best on stimuli that were neutral or mildly positive to begin with rather than stimuli a person already actively dislikes.

There is also a broader attribution lesson buried in this effect. We tend to attribute our liking for something to properties of the thing itself, "it's just a good song," rather than to the much less flattering and less obvious true cause, that we have simply encountered it many times before. That is its own small misattribution, a mismatch between the subjective feeling of liking and its real underlying cause, and it is a theme that will come up again when we look at how self-fulfilling prophecies get misread as evidence about a person's true nature rather than as an effect of expectations and repeated interaction.
